KEY MESSAGE 1...Dense river valley fog early this morning.

A combination of clearing skies, abundant low-level moisture in
part due to recent rain, and calm winds is resulting in areas of
fog this morning in the river valleys of western MD, eastern WV
and into the northern Shenandoah Valley in VA. Some of this fog
has become dense with visibility down to one quarter mile. Just
across the border in PA, some areas are seeing visibility as low
as just a few hundred feet.

Fog will likely persist/expand through daybreak before slowly
burning off. For now, a Dense Fog Advisory is in effect until 9
AM for Allegany, Garrett, Hampshire, and Mineral Counties where
dense fog is most widespread. But, this advisory may very well
need to be extended/expanded south and east.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Severe thunderstorms and some instances of 
flash flooding are possible on Sunday.

Some residual convective activity may be ongoing on Sunday 
morning. This remains to be seen and will be guided by the
degree of overnight instability and boundary placement. How the
atmosphere recovers through the day should ultimately dictate
the degree of severe thunderstorm threat during the core diurnal
heating hours. The ingredients are certainly present for a more
impactful event if meteorological parameters all come together.

Looking a bit more closely at this event, a broad mid/upper
ridge persist across the Four Corners eastward to the
southwestern Atlantic. Amplified flow north of this expansive
anticyclone will continue to be a conduit to active convection,
many in the form of mesoscale convective systems (MCS). As
mentioned above, a remnant MCS might still be ongoing early 
Sunday across the region. While above average heights persist, 
expect some non-zero height falls to cross the area in response 
to an approaching shortwave. Within this northwesterly flow 
aloft, vertical shear is ample for the time of year, generally 
around 30 to 35 knots. Depending on model choice, mixed-layer 
CAPE values approach 1,500 to 2,500 J/kg. The combination of 
these two will easily support a risk of severe weather. While 
damaging wind gusts are the most likely threat, other severe 
types loom if storms can remain discrete in nature.

Additionally, a Slight Risk for excessive rainfall continues
along much of the Alleghenies eastward along/north of I-66/U.S.
50. Precipitable water values rise markedly, possibly into the 2
to 2.25 inch range. While a single thunderstorm will be capable
of torrential downpours, the bigger threat would be for repeat
and/or training convection. The latter potential exists which
supports the flash flood risk. Although drought continues over
much of the region, many areas have seen a one category
improvement over the past week. Convection will likely be
ongoing into Sunday night with the cold front not passing
through until early Monday.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Seasonably warm conditions and daily shower and
thunderstorm chances are expected through Monday, before another
round of storms are possible on Thursday.

High pressure building across southern Quebec down into New
England will favor a mostly quiet day for the area today. An 
onshore component to the winds should favor a mix of clouds and 
sun through the day. Highs will rise into the mid/upper 80s with
any shower/thunderstorm chances confined to the Potomac 
Highlands across the central Shenandoah Valley toward I-64. 
Recent high-resolution models are showing an MCS racing across 
the Ohio Valley late today. Some of this could leak across the 
Alleghenies, but confidence is low given a fairly mixed model 
signal.

As Sunday's cold front tracks offshore, upper-level zonal flow 
bringing drier air from the Great Lakes persists over the Mid-
Atlantic through midweek, creating a break in the rain and 
thunderstorms. While temperatures & dewpoints drop a few degrees by 
Tuesday in the wake of the front, temperatures should gradually 
increase again in the latter half of the week as high pressure 
builds overhead. 

Meanwhile, an upper-level trough will begin to form over the 
Northern Plains and then track across the Great Lakes late in the 
week, with a strong cold front potentially moving through the Mid-
Atlantic between Thursday and Friday. Medium-range algorithms are 
already highlighting a potential for severe thunderstorms with this 
system. However, severe probabilities currently vary widely across 
models, with CSU ML probabilities highlighting only a marginal 5%-
15% probability as of the 12Z model runs while the WxNext2 Mean AI 
outlook is already showing a 30%-45% probability. Deterministically, 
the GFS/ECMWF also have not quite aligned on the timing and 
placement of the trough 7 days out. Should this setup
materialize, storms capable of heavy downpours and damaging 
winds would be possible. As drought conditions continue to
